utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth. Is everyone present? Yes. Once we resume, I'm going to ask the Office of the Prosecution to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis, Michael Keegan, and Kapila Waidyaratne appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. And now the Defence, in the order of the accused, will they please announce their names. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Defence of Mr. Kvocka, Mr. Lukic and co-defence Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kos is represented by Zarko Nikolic and Jelena Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning, I'm Toma Fila and together with Zoran Jovanovic we represent Mr. Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm attorney Simo Tosic from Banja Luka, my co-counsel Mr. Slobodan Stojanovic, attorney from Belgrade, and we represent Zoran Zigic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Jovan Simic, Dusan Masic, and Goran Rodic representing Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the accused Kvocka we have Lukic and Simic. And if I heard well, I didn't quite hear the first name of Mr. Prcac's attorney. Could you repeat your name, please? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Dubuisson, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is case number IT-98-30-T, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I see that Mr. Nikolic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the co-counsel's name has not entered the transcript, so could we correct that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat it, please? And in that way it will be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of the accused Kos consists of Mrs. Jelena Nikolic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, and Zarko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it now. Thank you very much. We're going to resume our case, and I now turn to Ms. Hollis. Is there a technical problem, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I want to make sure that the accused can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused, can you all follow us? Yes, I see a nod in the affirmative. Ms. Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution has filed a motion for clarification of various matters prior to the commencement of the Prosecution's case in chief. We believe that clarification of these matters will make the proceedings move more efficiently and more expeditiously. We would like to address these matters in turn as we have presented them in the motion, and different of those of us on the trial team will be dealing with each matter. Mr. Michael Keegan will be dealing with the first matter that we have raised in this motion, with permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, does the motion have to do with protective measures, the motion you filed on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the motion has to do with protective measures and a variety of other issues as well, including, Your Honours, a request that Your Honours take judicial notice of facts that have been presented to you; also a request that decisions be made concerning a motion for protective measures; also that clarification and decisions be made regarding the Prosecution's proposed procedure of using trial summaries and prior testimonies for witnesses. In addition to that, Your Honour, a discussion and decisions about the procedure on cross-examination. And finally, Your Honour, a request that a decision be made concerning the outstanding motion for a site visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was about to propose, and I think we envisaged a Status Conference for tomorrow. I don't know whether you agree, but perhaps we could deal with all those matters at the Status Conference tomorrow, and we could now immediately resume the proceedings. I don't know whether the questions you have mentioned, particularly the question regarding witnesses, perhaps we could deal with that matter today, and tomorrow we can address the whole motion at the Status Conference. Otherwise, there is a risk that we will be having a Status Conference rather than the trial hearing. What is your response to that suggestion, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, the Prosecution's understanding is that we would -- when we recommenced, the initial agenda item would be the Status Conference. We apologise if we misunderstood that, but that was our understanding, that the very first thing we would do would be to have a Status Conference and then move into presentation of evidence. Be that as it may, Your Honour, several of the things that I have mentioned do impact on all of the witnesses, such as the issue of trial summaries and prior testimony, the issue of cross-examination, and the issue also of protective measures does not apply to the first witness but does apply to the second, third, and fourth witnesses to be called. So the Prosecution would respectfully submit that it would, perhaps, be most efficient if we were to deal with the preliminary matters before resuming the witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is your witness present? You have witnesses ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have witnesses for this week, Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, we do not have a witness present at this moment because of our understanding about the Status Conference, but we would be able to bring the witness here very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long would you need to bring the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The witness is a short distance from here, so it would depend upon whether the witness is prepared to arrive, how long it would take them to prepare, and then bringing them here would be a matter of probably half an hour, Your Honour. So perhaps an hour, if we were to make the call now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, do you intend to make an opening statement in relation to Mr. Prcac before we recommence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there will be an opening statement regarding Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, has the Defence counsel received these various motions that you filed on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our understanding that they have. I can't speak for them, but that is our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I know that I didn't receive them, and I was here on the weekend. Yesterday was a holiday. I think that if there are many procedural, preliminary procedural matters that you, the Prosecution, believe should be decided, it's probably incumbent upon you to file earlier. We simply didn't receive those.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whose fault it is, but I think it's just a caution to file ahead of late Friday if it's a holiday weekend, because they were not delivered to us, and I personally would not be in a position to make an off-the-top of the head judgement without even reading your written materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. We understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, I think, Ms. Hollis, it would be a good idea to begin with the opening statement on Mr. Prcac. Then we could have a break, in order to get the witness here, and then we can begin with the testimony of the witness. And if he needs protective measures, we can decide on the spot, and tomorrow we can have the Status Conference at 1.30, I think we planned to have it. And that would give time for the Defence to prepare and for us also to study the material. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We will certainly comply with your wishes, Your Honour. As I said, two of the matters at least do impact on this witness as well. The first witness is not a protected witness, so there's no need for a decision on that. However, whether we will be allowed to use the prior testimony and whether we will be allowed to use trial summary will need to be decided for this witness, Your Honour. And I would ask Your Honour if we could be allowed to have our case manager depart the courtroom so that she can ensure that the witness is contacted and brought to the building immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We agree. We are granting permission for the assistant to leave. You can begin with your opening statement, Ms. Hollis. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Michael Keegan will be presenting the opening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The interpreters have requested a copy, and I need to apologise up front. Based on the discussions at the close of the last Status Conference we had, we anticipated, as we indicated, the Status Conference to begin with, and therefore we didn't bring the copies in this morning. So at this point, I'm sorry. I'll just endeavour to read very slowly. Your Honours, as this Chamber is aware, this case is about the ethnic cleansing and persecution of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in the area of the opstina of Prijedor. During the period alleged in the indictment, the accused Prcac, as with the other four accused in this case, participated in the brutal campaign orchestrated by the Bosnian Serb authorities in an effort to rid the region of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats as part of an effort to create a Serbian state. In particular, the accused Prcac knowingly participated in the crimes committed in the Omarska camp, one of the integral components of that brutal campaign. In the initial opening statement, my colleague, Grant Niemann, spoke to you of the who, when, where, and why of the crimes committed in opstina Prijedor, including those committed in the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps. He described for you the responsibility of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Zigic. With the joinder of the accused Prcac, we need to add him to the equation of criminal responsibility and to describe his participation in the campaign of terror that took place in opstina Prijedor between April and December 1992. The accused Prcac, along with the other four accused, is individually responsible for the crimes committed against the prisoners in the Omarska camp. In addition, Prcac, like the accused Kvocka, Kos, and Radic, held a position of superior authority but failed to prevent or to punish the mistreatment of prisoners by his subordinates. His criminal conduct, along with that of his co-accused, ensured that the vast majority of the non-Serb population that survived the attacks on their homes or their imprisonment in the camps would feel compelled to leave Prijedor. The conduct of the accused Prcac, like that of the other four accused, was a manifestation of collective criminality; that is, criminal conduct carried out by a group of individuals acting in pursuance of a common criminal design. The common criminal purpose or design that united the accused Prcac with the other four accused in this trial was the forced removal of the majority of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory claimed as Republika Srpska through a campaign of terror and persecution. To that end, the specific province of the accused Prcac and his co-accused was the Omarska camp. In that camp, the five co-accused subjected the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat prisoners, and the others who the Serb leadership associated with those two groups, to confinement under barbarous conditions. Prisoners were murdered, tortured, sexually assaulted, beaten, starved, and otherwise physically maltreated. Prisoners were also subjected to brutal interrogation sessions designed solely to create false confessions and false facts that could be used by the Bosnian Serb authorities as propaganda to justify their crimes and the ongoing persecution of the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. It is well recognised that members of a group engaged in a common criminal plan or design may contribute to the commission of the crime or crimes in different ways yet be held equally responsible for them. Some members of the group may physically perpetrate the criminal act or acts, while others may aid, abet, or otherwise facilitate the commission of the crimes. Despite the variations and the form of participation, however, the moral gravity or responsibility of each of the participants in the crime is often no different from one another. In the present case, the brutal crimes that were committed in the Omarska camp were directly assisted and facilitated by the conduct of the accused Prcac. While he may not have physically committed or perhaps not been physically present when each of the specific criminal acts alleged in the indictment or the attached schedules were committed, those criminal acts could not have been committed as they were without his assistance, approval, and acquiescence. Thus, the evidence will establish that the accused Prcac knowingly participated in the crimes committed in the Omarska camp by ordering, committing, and aiding and abetting the commission of those crimes through his approval, encouragement, and acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As my colleague described to you in the initial opening statement, there are three separate theories of responsibility under the "common purpose" doctrine that are applicable in this case. I will not repeat the full text of those arguments now; rather, I would refer the Chamber to the text of the prior opening address and the pre-trial brief submitted by the Prosecution regarding the accused Prcac. I would, however, like to summarise the three theories and address some of the facts that were not fully addressed earlier. The first theory of liability under the "common purpose" doctrine is where all the individuals involved in the criminal acts share the same criminal intention. The second theory is a specialised derivative of the first. It relates to what may be called, perhaps, the "criminal enterprise" doctrine and is related to the jurisprudence of the concentration camp cases which arose from the Second World War. That theory dictates that the accused must have known the nature of the criminal enterprise and had the intent to further its purpose. The third theory involves responsibility for criminal acts that may fall outside the original common design of the group. Under this theory, an accused may nevertheless be held criminally responsible if those acts were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the original criminal design. It is the Prosecution's position that the evidence will establish Dragoljub Prcac's criminal responsibility for the crimes charged beyond a reasonable doubt under any one or all three of the above theories. The evidence that will be presented will establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the common purpose of the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps was the brutal confinement of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and others who were identified with those groups until they were either killed or expelled from the Prijedor region. The evidence will prove that the camps were an essential component of the overall persecution of Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and others and played a major part in the ethnic cleansing of the Prijedor area. The evidence will prove that Mr. Prcac, along with the other co-accused, actively participated in this criminal enterprise: the Omarska camp. The evidence will show that through his conduct in the camp he followed, supported, and sustained the criminal conduct of the camp system. It is impossible that the accused Prcac, or any of the other co-accused, could have belonged to the staff of the Omarska camp for a substantial period of time, as they all did, without being aware of the criminal purpose and conduct of the camp system. It was equally impossible to hold positions of responsibility and authority for the operation of the Omarska camp, as this accused did, without being aware of the system, without being aware that on a daily basis prisoners in that camp were being murdered, raped, beaten, tortured, and starved to death. Faced with these clear facts, as it has already been made clear from the pre-trial submissions of the Defence, the accused, including Prcac, are trying to portray that they had no choice in their actions or that they had no real authority in the camp. The indications already before the Trial Chamber are that the Defence will try what is a fairly common tactic of Defence counsel, to place the blame on the dead guy, in this case, Simo Drljaca, the former chief of police, or another accused who is not present before this Chamber, Zeljko Meakic. The evidence in this case, however, clearly shows that this attempt to portray themselves as pawns in a system without rules or clear command structure falls without any merit. Rather, the evidence establishes, as anyone with a reasonable knowledge of the facts of this case would expect, that the crimes committed against the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats that are alleged in the indictment were executed pursuant to a well-devised plan and by forces that were well organised and structured. As to the question of whether a chain of command and the authority inherent therein existed in the Omarska police, that is, amongst those responsible for the camp, in the initial opening address, my colleague, Mr. Niemann, referred you to document 32A in the materials used for that address, which was a directive, dated 11 May 1992, from the chief of police in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca. That directive makes clear the strict organisation and chain of authority that existed. I quote: "The senior officer-policeman worker relationship is to be tightened to the maximum. All orders are to be acted upon without question. Any refusal to do so would result in termination or removal from the reserve forces." An example of the level of organisation and discipline that did, in fact, exist within the police forces and could be achieved when the superiors and the police forces wished to do so is evidenced by the bragging of Simo Drljaca and other SDS leaders after the takeover of Prijedor. That as a result of the outstanding organisation and discipline of the police forces, they took over power in the town of Prijedor in less than an hour, using a force of over 1500 men without firing a single shot. Finally, the evidence of the witnesses will establish beyond any doubt that there was a clear chain of command in the Omarska camp and that there was a clear -- and that the accused Prcac held the position of deputy commander, with the authority to control the conduct of the shift commanders, the guards, and visitors, such as the accused Zigic. He also had the authority to grant the prisoners more freedoms and rights within the camp, including access to potable water, reasonable living conditions, and hygienic standards, and contact with their families and friends to receive clothing, hygienic supplies, food, and medicines. As to the knowledge of the accused Dragoljub Prcac about the nature of the camp's operation and his criminal intention, the evidence shows that the accused knowingly participated in the crimes that occurred in the Omarska camp. During the commission of specific crimes in the camp, the accused Prcac would, at times, be present but would do nothing to stop the commission of those crimes. On many occasions he called out prisoners using lists that had been prepared. Those prisoners were then beaten or tortured or disappeared. He also permitted individuals from outside the camp, such as the accused Zigic, to regularly enter Omarska and to subject the prisoners to all forms of maltreatment, including murder. The accused Prcac, like Kvocka before him, manifested this conduct during a period when he had considerable authority, and indeed exercised the power of life and death over the prisoners in Omarska. The evidence will show that the accused Prcac moved around the camp and was seen in all areas, unlike the interrogators who apparently never moved around in the camp. As a result, the accused would have been intimately aware of the physical conditions of the prisoners and the appalling nature of the conditions they were existing in. The evidence will show that when the commander of the camp, Zeljko Meakic, was not in the camp, the accused Prcac was and served as the commander or senior man in charge. The evidence will show that before guards could act on certain requests from the prisoners, they had to check with the commander, Mr. Prcac. The evidence will show that the accused Prcac had the authority to direct where prisoners went in the camp, and if a guard disagreed, it was the accused's word that prevailed. Finally, the accused Prcac's failure to take reasonable steps to prevent the crimes that were occurring or to try to punish those that committed them, or to alter the conditions of the confinement of the prisoners, was a calculated disregard of his obligations as a policeman in Bosnia-Herzegovina and those of a superior in the Omarska camp. Such a cruel omission or failure to exercise his obligations also created a powerful inference of intent to participate in the repressive system. It is also relevant to recall that full loyalty to the SDS and its programmes was a requirement to hold any position of authority in any sector of government or the economy at that time, including the police service. The position of the deputy commander of one of the most important camps was no small position. As the deputy commander of the camp, Mr. Prcac's presence and his total failure to restrain the guards' misconduct could have only encouraged the continued abuse of prisoners by guards and so-called visitors to the camp, such as the accused Zigic. By standing by and providing this encouragement, Mr. Prcac voluntarily participated in the common criminal design that was the Omarska camp. Moreover, by presiding over such criminal acts, the accused demonstrated his intent that they occur. The result of his approval, encouragement, and acquiescence in the conduct of the guards and visitors, such as Zigic, at Omarska was manifested in the many crimes that were committed there, including, in the latter part of July, the murder of a great number of prisoners who had been captured in what's been referred to as the Brdo region, on the left bank of the Sana River in the opstina Prijedor. After those prisoners arrived in the camp, they were subjected to brutal beatings and many were killed. The Omarska prison camp was at the vanguard of the Bosnian Serb system of persecution and ethnic cleansing. The day-to-day participation in and support for the crimes that were committed in the Omarska camp is evidence of the accused Prcac's intent to participate in this system. The accused Prcac, along with the other accused in this matter, shared the common criminal design to persecute Muslims and Croats in the Prijedor region so as to cleanse that region of those who would not participate in the Serbian state. Finally, the pervasive nature of the cruelty, violence, and disregard for human life that existed in the Omarska camp on a daily basis dictates that all of the particular acts of violence and the crimes alleged in the indictment fell within the natural, foreseeable, and horrible consequences of the operation of the Omarska camp. The accused's continued and knowing participation in the operation of the Omarska camp makes him criminally responsible for all of the acts alleged. In summation, the evidence presented during this trial will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Prcac, along with the other four accused, shared a common criminal purpose, the forced removal of a majority of the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory claimed as Republika Srpska through a campaign of terror and persecution. To that end, the accused Prcac and his co-accused, through their actions in the Omarska camp, actively participated in this common design, and in doing so bears responsibility for the crimes against humanity and violations of the laws of war that are charged in the indictment, both as an individual and as a superior for his failure to take reasonable steps to prevent the crimes from occurring or for failing to punish those who committed the crimes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Keegan. I think that we are now going to have a break. Ms. Hollis, have you received any information regarding the availability of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is available here, but I've received no indication as to how quickly the witness will be in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 25-minute break, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Ms. Hollis, you have the floor, and we have the motions. Excuse me. Mr. Simic, do you wish to say something? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not intend to enter a debate as regards the opening statement of Mr. Keegan. However, I should like to expose one objection of the Defence as a whole. Mr. Keegan made an allegation during his opening statement which may be a result of either misinterpretation or a misunderstanding. He stated that the accused are trying to place the blame on Mr. Meakic, that is, to place the blame on some other persons. I have to say that we have submitted preliminary briefs that the accused have been interviewed, that Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic have testified, and I have to say that not at one point did they ever try to put the blame on Mr. Meakic. They were simply trying to explain the status of Mr. Meakic, who was the commander of the police station in Omarska. And the Prosecutor himself has quoted the relevant decision in his opening statement a number of times. We have to stress this because this may have some adverse consequences for the Defence. This is a public trial and we have to stress this, we have to make this objection so as to avoid any adverse effect on the Defence and any damage that may be caused to our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Keegan, do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was more of a rhetorical objection. We have a witness here in the courtroom, but it seems that Mr. Tosic has something to say. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to put forth several facts. I don't know whether the witness should remain in the courtroom. This is something that I want to say before the testimony of the witness. I should like the Court to ask the witness to leave the courtroom because I have something to say which bears on the preliminary matters as regards the presentation of evidence. I did not want to interrupt Mr. Keegan in his opening statement, but I should like to speak now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic, would it be possible for you to make your comment after the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to say that before the beginning of the testimony, because I believe that certain facts and certain circumstances should be clarified before this witness begins his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Tosic, you understand the proceedings. It is very difficult to bring the witness in the courtroom and then ask him to leave the courtroom. I mean, this does not seem serious, a serious way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you do not think that the witness should leave the courtroom, well, let him stay in the courtroom. But I have to stress certain facts which bear upon his testimony. I personally do not have anything against his staying in the courtroom. Perhaps when I say what I have to say, you will see whether it is necessary for the witness to leave the courtroom or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, do you have any information as regards the intervention of Mr. Tosic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would suggest that to avoid any appearance that the witness' testimony may be prejudiced by what he may hear, that indeed if there are preliminary matters, that he be asked to leave the courtroom so that those preliminary matters can be discussed. That way, Your Honour, there would not even be an appearance that this witness' testimony was somehow influenced by whatever it is that Mr. Tosic wishes to raise. So we would agree with Mr. Tosic that caution would make it the better practice for the witness to leave the courtroom while he raises whatever concerns he has. In addition, Your Honour, we do note that, of course, the Defence has an opportunity to make an open in response to ours, and since we did make an additional open, we take Mr. Tosic's remarks to be basically in a form of an opening in response to ours. It could be that other of these Defence counsel also wish to make similar remarks. If they do, of course it is for Your Honours to determine whether they may do so. But again, we believe it would be better for this issue to be dealt with outside the presence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have to apologise for this, but we have to ask you to leave the courtroom for a short period of time, and afterwards you will be back. Thank you very much for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic, it is always possible to tell the Judges that you intend to say something before the witness is brought in. I think that this is the procedure that should be observed. If there is a motion, it has to be made orally, after having consulted the other party. In that way, we can proceed in a more efficient manner. And now you have the floor, Mr. Tosic. Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our position is the following: We do not wish to have testimony of the witness before a Status Conference, and I think that the reasons will justify our motion. As regards the indictment; namely, the amended indictment with Mr. Prcac, we have not yet received it. I do not think that any changes in terms of identity have been added to the indictment. What we have now is the indictment from July 1999, and in accordance with Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we believe that this indictment should be made available to us; namely, the amended indictment. We do not wish to obstruct the proceedings in any way. I shall say that we will waive our right to object to the amended indictment. However, I must stress that we do not have the amended indictment. We assumed that no changes as regards the identity have been added to the indictment, and I believe that the charges have remained the same as regards my client. However, I must say that I have not seen the amended indictment, neither has my client. And we believe that this amended indictment should be made available to the Defence before the presentation of evidence, before we start with the testimony of the witness. Furthermore, as regards the facts -- non-contested facts, there are 444 of them, and I am not in a position to state our view of the facts. We have already discussed them during the last Status Conference, but I have to say that I do not -- I don't know what these facts are all about. I haven't received a copy of the translation. I don't know whether we're talking about some new facts or whether these are the previous 583 facts, or if this is a summary of the facts that we have already received. As regards the motion submitted by the Prosecutor, dated February 2000, we are not familiar with the contents of the motion and we cannot state our position. The Prosecutor has suggested that we should use trial summaries from some other cases. I have to say that we have received only a list of witnesses. I can only surmise as to the identity of the witness that we have today in the courtroom, but that is all. I think that we should have been provided with a list of witnesses at least one week beforehand so that we could prepare ourselves in a timely fashion for our defence. As far as I know, the witness who has just left the courtroom, Mr. Emir Beganovic, testified in the Tadic case. I do not know what the position of the Chamber is. The Prosecutor has requested that the testimony from the Tadic case should be admitted. But I still don't know whether we should be allowed to cross-examine the witness in question. So these are the circumstances that should be dealt with at the Status Conference. These are the matters that should be taken care of before we begin with the testimony of the witness. That is what I had to say, Your Honour. If I may add just one thing. The documents I have referred to have not been translated, witness summaries, trial summaries, nor the facts, adjudicated facts. I don't know about my colleagues, but I have received the relevant documentation only this morning. So I don't think that it would be appropriate for us to begin with the testimony of the witness before we have resolved all the procedural matters. I think it is inappropriate that we should not have the amended indictment and that we should be using the indictment dated from the previous year. We have five accused here, and I think that all of the Defence counsel should be made familiar with the amended indictment. I'm speaking on behalf of my client, but also on behalf of the Defence as a whole. We do not intend to object to the indictment or to obstruct the proceedings in any way. We will waive our right to do that. But we are simply asking for this indictment to be made available for us. We need some time to read it, and afterwards we will state officially that we will waive our right to object to the indictment. We need to know that nothing of a significance has been changed. And again I must stress that it is highly inappropriate for us to discuss something that we have not seen. I wanted this matter to be entered in the record, to be made part of the record, before we start with the proceedings of the presentation of evidence. There is a number of things that have to be dealt with prior to the testimony of the witness. It is all the same for us as regards the timing of the testimony, whether we should begin today or tomorrow, but these are matters that cannot be circumvented or bypassed. We have seen the witness but we don't know exactly about his identity. We are from the relevant area, and that's why we happened to know who the witness is. But you said that I should have addressed the Chamber beforehand, before the witness enters the courtroom. But we were simply not in a position to do so because we didn't know who would be the next witness. It is only at the beginning of the session -- I believe that we should enter the courtroom first and that only then the witness should be called in. I did not wish to interrupt the proceedings before the break because Mr. Keegan was having his opening statement, and I don't think that it was appropriate for the witness to be brought into the courtroom before we have settled all the procedural matters as regards the presentation of evidence. On the other hand, I do object on the course of action taken by the Prosecutor. I think that it was necessary for us to be informed about the witness who was supposed to testify today. I know that we have had enough time to prepare ourselves, but we should have made -- we should have been informed about the identity of the witness. We should have been told explicitly that Emir Beganovic would testify. We cannot surmise as to the order of witnesses. We do not know, for example, who will be the next witness tomorrow. If we finish the testimony of this witness in half an hour, we are not in a position to know anything about the next witness. And there are a number of things that we have to discuss with our clients, things that they may have remembered in the meantime and that concern the relevant witness. Therefore, I think that all these matters should be resolved at a Status Conference, as has been suggested by Ms. Hollis, and then only after that, that we should begin with the presentation of evidence; namely, the testimony of various witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tosic. We have to have in mind the need to proceed in a speedy and efficient manner, and we wanted to have a joinder of the accused in this case, we wanted to proceed with the accused Prcac, and we thought that you would be ready for the proceedings. It is true that we announced a Status Conference, but maybe it was not clear whether the Status Conference would take place at the beginning or at the end of the week. But be that as it may, I shall now give the floor to Ms. Hollis, to give her an opportunity to respond to the motion by the Defence. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll try to touch on all the different matters that were raised by Defence counsel. Involving the amended indictment, of course, the procedure that was followed is we had a joinder, as you indicated, and the Court ruled on a joinder. It is the Prosecution's understanding that, indeed, the Defence has a copy of the Prcac indictment, so indeed they have a copy of the indictments on which we are proceeding. That's our first point as to the indictment. So, indeed, they do have a copy of the relevant indictments on which we're proceeding in this case. Secondly, regarding the facts that were submitted, it is the Prosecution's understanding that as of our last discussion, we were asked to provide again the facts that had been agreed upon by all the parties with another cover sheet and another filing. We did that. So that, indeed, what has been provided to this counsel are the facts that they have previously agreed to, and that was filed on the 28th. But the facts are the same that have been agreed to since the Status Conference on the 24th of February, with the four accused previously in the case, and the facts that the Defence counsel for Mr. Prcac agreed to in our Status Conference regarding him. Your Honour, as to the motion we referred to of February of 2000, the Defence should have been, and we believe were, served a copy of that motion when it was filed. So we believe they would have that motion in their possession and could have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Hollis. Which motion? You just gave us the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the counsel is referring to a motion which we adopt as part of our argument on judicial notice, and that would have been a motion that we did file. It would have been a motion that should have been served on the counsel, and we believe that they had it when we had our previous discussions on judicial motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does that include the requests in your current motion? I did get a chance to get a hold of it during the recess. Your request in the current motion that the Chamber make findings based on the judicial notice?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recollection is that that matter was raised in our Status Conference on the 24th of February with the Defence counsel present. The motion prior to that I don't believe may have addressed that particular point. But that matter was raised in February in our Status Conference at which these counsel were present. Your Honour, regarding the list of witnesses, the current order of witnesses, a courtesy copy of that was placed in the lockers for four of the accused counsel on Thursday evening. The order was filed on Friday, the 28th. The counsel for Mr. Prcac had a locker but the guard at this security -- outside security desk did not have the number of the locker. So on Thursday evening, the 27th, we were unable to put the courtesy copy into his locker. But the very next morning, at the beginning of business, a courtesy copy was provided to the Defence unit to be provided to counsel for Mr. Simic. So service was made of a courtesy copy on four of the counsel on the evening of 27 April and the notice was filed on the 28th, and a courtesy copy was provided through the Defence unit to Mr. Prcac's counsel. So indeed since Friday, at least, counsel would have known who our first witness is, and that's Mr. Emir Beganovic, as it is listed on that order. In regard to objections about trial summaries, trial transcripts, the first witness is a witness for whom we will be offering both a trial summary and a trial transcript. So perhaps it is appropriate to deal with that matter before the witness is brought back in. In regard to the translation of these items, Your Honours, our understanding is that Rule 66 sets forth two categories of disclosure that must be provided in a language the accused understands. The first of those is the confirmation material. That was done. The second of those are statements of witnesses we intend to call. That has been done. The trial summaries, we do not believe, are statements of the witnesses, and we have not provided those in B/C/S. The adjudicated facts and other motions, there is no requirement we're aware of that we provide those in B/C/S. Indeed, Your Honours, it is our understanding that one of the requirements for counsel to practice before this Tribunal is that at least someone on the team is able to operate in one of the two languages of the Tribunal. So to the extent that is a problem, perhaps we should address that early on in the case. But we believe we have provided the appropriate materials in the language of the accused, and the other types of materials that Defence counsel addresses, in our opinion, do not have to be provided to the counsel in B/C/S. Your Honour, if I have failed to address any of the points, please remind me and I will address them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question. In your opinion, will inquiry, and particularly cross-examination, of the witness who's now waiting outside involve some of the requests you made for the way in which cross-examination should be required and limited, which I've only had a chance to glance at at the recess?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We believe that it will for all of these witnesses, even those without prior testimony, because of the number of Defence counsel who will be questioning the witness. So again that is a procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That is something which Defence counsel got, they did get that motion which contains that requested limits or order of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was filed on Friday, Your Honour. That is part of the additional matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's in the same motion with the summaries, but I don't know whether they've had a chance to look at it or not before they began any --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect to the Prosecution, I personally never received the indictment for Mr. Prcac. I don't know about other Defence counsel. But I have not received it, nor my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, but the indictment is a public act, a public document, isn't it, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, it is a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the second matter, the generally established facts, it is not true that all of us Defence counsel, before Mr. Prcac joined us, agreed with those facts. As far as I know, out of the 583, Mr. Simic and I did not agree with a large number of those facts. So that we cannot accept the statement by Ms. Hollis that we have agreed on all those facts. As for the order of witnesses, I agree, we were given a list of witnesses but no additional information to tell us whether the Prosecution will abide by that order of witnesses. So if that is the final list in which the witnesses will be called, then I hope we will be so informed. As for the translation issue, we received mostly the English, not even the French versions, and as far as I know, not one of my colleagues, or our clients, have received the motions or these facts or any other documents in our own language. I apologise. We received the French version and not the English version. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I can see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had not intended to join in this discussion, but we were promised that we would be given statements by two witnesses today, and we haven't received that. They are Witnesses AG and AH, completely new witnesses who were never mentioned before, and we were told in the motion submitted by the Prosecution, given to us on Friday night -- I must point out that we had a weekend and we had a holiday yesterday, our clients have been in detention for two years, and suddenly we're given these documents are given to us overnight. But these statements were promised to us, and to this moment, we haven't received those statements. We haven't received another nine statements which were due to us. I am not trying to criticise anybody, but you will receive my response to what I received Friday night. But, you know, it is rather difficult for all of us to get together and agree on our responses. Otherwise, the trial will last very long. And we must have time, at least 24 hours, to study things. Even the promised statements have not reached me of those two witnesses. And I think that we should respect one another's words. I think you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be better to say -- to hear the Defence and then have the response of the Prosecution. Otherwise we'll never leave here. Mr. Nikolic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to briefly join in this discussion regarding certain points that have been raised here. The motions of the Prosecution are dated the 28th of April. That is when a list of witnesses was submitted which differs significantly from the previous list of proposed witnesses and which were covered by the Prosecution's motion compiled in accordance with Rule 65 ter. This new motion, with the new list of witnesses, was not compiled in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 ter. We received last night, in our locker, something that looks like that and which is also dated the 28th of April; however, at first glance are these technical errors or something, but they do take time. Jasmir Okic is mentioned here under number 12. In the list of witnesses, he comes under number 9. All the other numbering of witnesses from this motion, which should correspond to 65 ter, does not correspond to the numbering in the list of witnesses submitted on the 28th of April, except for the two last ones. Secondly, no where is mention made of which circumstances the witness is going to testify and in reference to which accused, as required by the provisions of Rule 65 ter. So these are problems confronting the Defence, especially now, two days prior to trial, and I will use the words used by Judge Wald when she said, "It isn't reasonable," because we had quite a long recess, and the Defence could have studied all these things in a timely fashion, instead of talking about them now, documents that we received last night. There are 444 adjudicated facts. Just to look through that list requires time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I think now we have to give the floor to Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I had not intended to speak, but as the discussion is broadening, I feel it necessary to express my position. Indeed, it is rather unusual, after two years of preparations, that we should encounter so many technical errors on the part of the Prosecution. However, if the Trial Chamber rules that we should hear Mr. Beganovic as a witness, since he is already here, I would suggest that today we have the examination-in-chief in the classical manner, without tendering the transcript or the summary, that we respect the Rules, and only as of future witnesses we apply the Rules that may be adopted tomorrow at the Status Conference. We would indeed like this trial to be as efficient as possible, that we avoid any waste of time, because after all, this is a serious case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Mr. Jovan Simic now. Do you have any observations or comments to make? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would not really have anything much to add to what my colleagues have said. But I would like to say, regarding the witnesses that apply to my client, I have not received all the statements -- I do not have the statements of the witnesses who are going to testify about my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have made disclosure to Mr. Prcac's counsel. We have continued to make disclosure to Mr. Prcac's counsel. And we are aware that there are some statements, and I'm not -- I can't tell you at this moment how many, that need to be provided in the B/C/S. The translation unit, which is not part of the Office of the Prosecutor, is working on that. We do not have those. But to say he has not received statements of witnesses relevant to his client, we suggest, is not correct. Any witness who testifies about what happened in Omarska camp during the period Mr. Prcac was there is a witness relevant to Mr. Prcac, at least in the Prosecution's submission. In regard to the issue of the translations, again that comes back to what is required for us to provide in B/C/S and what other kinds of documents the Defence may need to have in B/C/S. We believe we have complied, with a few exceptions, with our requirement to provide the documents in B/C/S that are required of us. If the Defence counsel are having difficulties because they do not have the material in a language that they understand, that needs to be raised and it needs to be sorted out; we agree with that. But that is not a matter that is the responsibility of the Prosecution. And again we believe it needs to be sorted out in light of the practice rules for Defence counsel who appear before this Tribunal. Mr. Emir Beganovic was listed as our number 1 witness in a notice to the Defence. It was given to them on the 6th of March. Now, our witness list did change, and indeed, on the 28th we did file a notice, and it was a notice of change of witness list. And as I mentioned before, they were given -- four of the accused counsel were given a copy of that the night before we filed it, and counsel for Mr. Prcac was given a courtesy copy of that Friday morning through the Defence unit. So we did provide that. We also provided the transcript of the prior testimony of Mr. Beganovic in the lockers, and that was provided -- that may have been provided over the weekend, Your Honour. And I'm not sure I have addressed all of those issues. But, indeed, the witness order was made known to them. We did provide the materials, at least over the weekend, for them regarding Emir Beganovic. With regard to witnesses who were referred to as AG and AH, those witnesses are witnesses who have particular circumstances and we indicated that we would provide the statements relevant to those witnesses once we have a decision about protective measures. We did not provide it to the counsel prior to them because we want the Trial Chamber to act on protective measures before we disclose to the Defence the identity of those two witnesses. They are not witnesses that are in our first four or five or six who will be called, and that is the reason that they were not provided those statements. And we indicated that we would be providing them when we had the Status Conference, which I as I mentioned earlier, the Prosecution believed would have been the first order of business for us today. Your Honours, if there are other matters that I have not addressed, if you will ask me any questions you have, I will address them. Your Honour, also one final thing about why, at this late date, we are changing witness orders, that will be raised in the protective measures motion tomorrow, or whenever we deal with that, because the Prosecution feels a very compelling need to inform this Trial Chamber of the various difficulties potential witnesses are having in this case. And we will take that, I believe, more appropriately in a private or closed session. But that is the primary reason for the change in our witness list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, let me get your reaction to the Defence counsel, Mr. Simic's, I think, proposal that for the remainder of today we might take the first witness on direct and then reserve the questions raised in your motions for tomorrow's Status Conference when they can hopefully be decided. Is that a doable scenario from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are certainly areas that are not covered by the prior testimony that we could begin with today, and then once we determine prior testimony, we will know whether we need to lead that evidence or not. So we could certainly make a start with this witness before introducing the prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that we can all see that it is always more difficult to get started again, because, after all, all of us, the Judges and the Defence, received a large pile of documents on Friday and we saw them for the first time during the break. What the Chamber had planned was to make the best of the time, and we thought that by hearing testimony would be a way to do that, and then to have a Status Conference at which we can discuss matters and deal with them. So we have two possibilities now: either we discuss the motion for protective measures in order to begin the testimony with all the witnesses, or we begin only with the examination-in-chief of this witness and deal with all the other matters afterwards. So in any event, as we had planned to have the Status Conference tomorrow, at 3.30, that is, after the normal working day, perhaps it is too late now because we have to do something tomorrow morning. And also there's the problem of witnesses and their position, because they're here and waiting. Perhaps, however, in order to be more efficient, it would be better to have a discussion on the motion now regarding the protection of witnesses and then we could be ready for tomorrow, and all the other matters could be discussed at the Status Conference tomorrow at 3.30. I should like, however, to hear Ms. Hollis and perhaps the Defence as a reaction to what I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because Witnesses 2, 3, and 4 are the subject of our written motion for protective measures, or will be the subject of oral motions for protective measures, we agree that it would be expeditious to deal with that motion today. That way, we wouldn't have to interrupt proceedings tomorrow when we call Witness number 2 and possibly number 3. We do agree with that suggestion, that we deal with that motion today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. I should like to confer with each of Defence counsel quickly. Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I support the proposal that we deal with this matter today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is the one I presented a moment ago, that is, that we first deal with all the procedural matters and then hear the testimony of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should have a short break for the Defence to be able to familiarise themselves with this motion, after which we will resume work and make the best of all the time at our disposal, until 2.30, to discuss this motion for protective measures and possibly to deal with other matters as well, if possible. So I'm making this break for us to be able to reorganise a little, and if I may suggest that we have the discussion in closed session. Is that agreeable, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would request that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm saying that for the benefit of the public, so that when we will be talking about protective measures, we are going to have a closed hearing after the break. And the break will be for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 12.27 p.m., to be followed by a Status Conference 21 22 23 24 25
